clue.text: One served Scottish king, for example

definitions.text: One served Scottish king, for example

blocks.note: surface reading: a servant or courtier who waited on a king of Scotland
setter's reading: the creature whose repeated attempts to climb its thread set Robert the Bruce an example of perseverance

explanation.walkthrough: 'Served' suggests a servant at table, but the service here was setting an example: the legend has a defeated Robert the Bruce, hiding in a cave, inspired to try again by a web-spinner that kept trying.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Scottish legend this small eight-legged weaver gave King Robert the lesson in persistence that preceded Bannockburn.

clue.text: President has a dance

blocks.note: James K. Polk, eleventh President of the United States
taken as written

explanation.surface: A head of state takes to the dance floor.
explanation.definitionFit: The polka is a lively Bohemian couple dance in two-four time, popular across nineteenth-century Europe.

clue.text: Ready, perhaps, to change? That's the ticket!

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the word before it is only one possible arrangement, so its letters may be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
to turn is to change, as the tide or the weather turns

explanation.surface: Someone poised to make a change is told cheerily that this is exactly the right thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's the ticket!' is the idiom for 'just the thing', but read literally it points at a ticket. A day return is a British rail ticket out and back on the same day.
explanation.definitionFit: A day return is a kind of railway ticket, valid for an outward and homeward journey on one day.

clue.text: Don informed of Jane Eyre's marriage

blocks.note: first meaning: a university teacher, in Britain a rank just below professor
second meaning: the one told the news in Charlotte Bronte's famous line opening the novel's final chapter

explanation.walkthrough: Jane Eyre's last chapter begins 'Reader, I married him', so the person informed of her marriage is whoever is holding the book. In British universities a reader is a senior academic, a don.
explanation.definitionFit: A reader is both a senior British university lecturer and the person Jane addresses directly when announcing her wedding to Rochester.

clue.text: How it used to be - ungrammatically, so to speak

definitions.text: How it used to be - ungrammatically

blocks.clueFragment: How it used to be - ungrammatically
blocks.note: first meaning: a past state of affairs put with the wrong verb form, 'were' where standard grammar says 'was'
second meaning: a phrase softening a figurative expression

explanation.surface: A speaker admits that their account of the old days is a little loose, in grammar and in meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally the phrase means 'as it was', with 'were' standing in ungrammatically for 'was'; as an idiom it means 'in a manner of speaking'.
explanation.definitionFit: The fixed phrase is used to signal that the words are figurative, exactly like the filler 'so to speak'.

clue.text: Book long sca-voyage

definitions.note: the scan reads sca where the paper printed sea

blocks.note: first meaning: E. M. Forster's 1924 novel of British India
second meaning: read literally, the title describes a lengthy trip by ship to the subcontinent; sca is a scanning error for sea

explanation.surface: Someone books a long cruise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a verb, as in reserving a cruise, but it is the noun: a novel whose title also describes a voyage from Britain to India.
explanation.definitionFit: Forster's novel takes its name from Whitman's poem, and literally names the weeks-long crossing by ship from England to Bombay.

clue.text: Peril not, sorted out for multinational organization

indicators.note: things sorted out are put into a new order, so the preceding letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A danger is dealt with by an international body.
explanation.definitionFit: Interpol is the international criminal police organisation through which many member countries' police forces cooperate.

clue.text: Tricks I left captured by bridge players

indicators.note: something captured is held inside its captors, so the first letters sit within the others

blocks.note: West, East and South, three of the four seats at a bridge table
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: At the card table, a player leaves after being outwitted by tricks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tricks' sounds like the tricks won at bridge, but it is the definition: crafty ploys.
explanation.definitionFit: Wiles are cunning stratagems used to deceive or persuade, so they are tricks in the sense of artful manoeuvres.

clue.text: Surviving once part of county dismissed

blocks.note: Yorkshire was divided into three Ridings until local government reorganisation in 1974
a batsman dismissed in cricket is out

explanation.surface: A former district of a shire is abolished.
explanation.walkthrough: A riding was one of the administrative thirds of Yorkshire, England's largest county; 'once' reflects their abolition in 1974.
explanation.definitionFit: To ride out a storm or crisis is to come through it safely, so the phrase means getting through hardship unscathed.

clue.text: Actively contributes - at some stage?

blocks.note: first meaning: takes an active share in an undertaking
second meaning, punning: takes on a role in a play, on a theatre stage

explanation.walkthrough: 'At some stage' normally means at some point in time; the question mark invites reading 'stage' as a theatre's.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for contributing to an outcome is borrowed from acting, where a performer takes on a role in a production.

clue.text: Game acceptable in Liberal party

indicators.note: in places one item within the letters that follow it

blocks.note: L is the standard abbreviation for Liberal
U means upper-class, hence socially acceptable
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: A sport finds approval at a political party's gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: U and non-U were 1950s labels for upper-class and not-quite-acceptable usage, so U means acceptable.
explanation.definitionFit: Ludo is a simple board game in which counters race round the board on throws of a die.

clue.text: Indescribable confusion of salesmen

indicators.note: confusion is a jumbled state, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written, eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A crowd of sales staff descends into chaos beyond words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nameless is too dreadful or vague to be given a name, so it cannot be put into words.

clue.text: Originating revolt

blocks.note: first meaning: coming up or springing from
second meaning: a rebellion or uprising

explanation.walkthrough: Two unrelated senses: the participle, as a river rises at its source, and the noun, as in the Easter Rising.
explanation.definitionFit: A river is said to rise where it originates, and a rebellion against authority is an uprising.

clue.text: Roundabout way, say, to use language

indicators.note: round about means placed all around, so the way is enclosed by what surrounds it

blocks.note: TENTATIVE: most likely the two U-turns of a roundabout route, U being the sign for a turn back; nothing else in the clue supplies these letters
Rd is the abbreviation for road, an example of a way, which is what say signals

explanation.surface: A circuitous road is a good way into using a language.
explanation.walkthrough: This parse is uncertain: RD for a road is secure, but how the clue supplies the U on each side is a best guess, a road with a U-turn at either end.
explanation.definitionFit: Urdu is the national language of Pakistan, also widely spoken in northern India.

clue.text: Spoil woman's meat in Northern town

blocks.note: to rot is to go bad, to spoil
the possessive pronoun for a woman
ham is cured pork

explanation.surface: A woman's joint of meat goes off in a town up north.
explanation.walkthrough: Rotherham is a South Yorkshire town in the north of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotherham is a former steel and coal town in South Yorkshire, in the North of England.

clue.text: Course satisfactory to conductor

blocks.note: good means satisfactory
Sir Henry Wood, the conductor who founded the Proms

explanation.surface: A course of study meets a bandleader's approval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' suggests a meal or study, but here it is a racecourse: Goodwood, in West Sussex, England. Sir Henry Wood founded London's Proms concerts.
explanation.definitionFit: Goodwood is a horse-racing course in West Sussex, home of the summer meeting known as Glorious Goodwood.

clue.text: Ace flew round when scrambled

indicators.note: scrambled means mixed up, so the letters before it are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A fighter pilot circled when the squadron was scrambled for action.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is wartime flying: an ace is a top pilot, and a squadron is scrambled when ordered into the air. Here 'Ace' is the slang adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: As slang adjectives, ace and wonderful both mean excellent or first-rate.

clue.text: Informs papers: one's in a mess

indicators.note: things in a mess are disordered, so the combined letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
one is I, and the apostrophe-s stands for is

explanation.surface: The newspapers inform you, but someone's desk is chaotic.
explanation.definitionFit: To apprise someone is to tell or notify them of something, a formal synonym for informing.

clue.text: Nasty type returns best woollen garments

indicators.note: something that returns goes back the way it came, so the following words are read from the end

blocks.note: top means best
knits are knitted woollen clothes

explanation.surface: An unpleasant person brings back the finest jumpers.
explanation.definitionFit: Stinkpot is a dated term of abuse for a contemptible or unpleasant person, much like stinker.

clue.text: A flat, for example, to see

blocks.note: first meaning: A flat is a musical pitch, one of many
second meaning: to notice or observe

explanation.walkthrough: 'A flat' looks like an apartment, but it is the musical pitch A-flat.
explanation.definitionFit: A-flat is a single musical pitch, and to note something is to notice or observe it.

clue.text: Recently acquired EEC capital

blocks.note: surface reading: money newly gained by the European Economic Community
setter's reading: the capital city of a nation that had recently joined the EEC

explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' reads as funds, but it is a capital city. Greece joined the European Economic Community in 1981, four years before this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek capital became a European Community capital city when Greece joined the Common Market in 1981.

clue.text: Very little for one of the hired mourners

blocks.note: wee is Scottish for small
per means for, as in ten per box

explanation.surface: Hardly anything is paid to a professional mourner.
explanation.walkthrough: In Victorian funerals, weepers were paid to walk with the coffin and display grief.
explanation.definitionFit: A weeper was a person paid to grieve visibly at funerals, a professional mourner.

clue.text: Nation minimally in debt?

blocks.note: p, a penny, is the smallest sum in British money
an ower is one who owes, someone in debt

explanation.surface: A country with only a tiny deficit, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: someone owing only a penny is a 'p-ower'.
explanation.definitionFit: A power is a state with influence in world affairs, as in great power or superpower.

clue.text: Current not connected to earth?

blocks.note: first meaning: generally felt or rumoured, as ideas that are about
second meaning, literally: aloft, off the ground

explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' and 'earth' together suggest electrical wiring, but the current is the adjective for what is prevalent, and the second half is literal: airborne.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideas or feelings that are widely sensed are said to be in the air, and something airborne is literally not touching the ground.

clue.text: People - or their rulers, in certain cases

blocks.note: first meaning: the Quechua-speaking nation of the Andean empire
second meaning: the title of that empire's emperor, held by a succession of rulers

explanation.surface: A nation, or in some instances those who rule it.
explanation.walkthrough: The name was first the title of the Sapa Inca, the emperor, and was later extended by the Spanish to the whole people.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andean empire's people are known by the title originally borne by its supreme rulers in Cuzco.

clue.text: Make appearance in entertainment

blocks.note: first meaning: to turn up or become visible
second meaning: a performance or spectacle

explanation.surface: Turning up for a part in a performance.
explanation.definitionFit: To show is informal for to turn up, and a show is a theatrical performance or spectacle.

clue.text: Team to accomplish unexpected result

blocks.note: a side is a team in sport
to effect a change is to bring it about

explanation.surface: A squad pulls off a surprise result.
explanation.definitionFit: A side effect is a secondary, usually unintended consequence, as of a medicine.

clue.text: Perishers didn't have this first-class fare

definitions.text: Perishers didn't have this first-class fare

blocks.clueFragment: Perishers didn't have this first-class fare
blocks.note: surface reading: some poor wretches went without a top-class meal or ticket
setter's reading: mortals, those who perish, never tasted the food of the immortal gods

explanation.walkthrough: 'Perishers' is British slang for rascals, but read literally it means those who die, mortals. In Greek myth only the gods ate this food, which kept them immortal.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambrosia was the food of the Olympian gods, conferring immortality and denied to mortal humans.

clue.text: Extravagant display put up by diver

blocks.note: first meaning: a showy show of spending, as in making a big one
second meaning: the spray of water thrown up when someone dives in

explanation.surface: A diver puts on a lavish show.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a splash is to attract attention lavishly, and the water thrown up by an entering diver is literally that.
